answers.justification: C1 shows early-action yield, with decisions released on the old timetable and merit files at a 16-day median, fell by the same amount (45.2→37.8, −7.4pp) as regular-decision yield (39.0→31.5, −7.5pp), where merit files took 38 days; both rounds had about the same merit-eligible share, so slower RD turnaround explains none of the extra drop (E2, C1).

C2 shows yield fell about 13pp only in the Dean's and Merit tiers, whose awards were cut, while the unchanged Presidential and no-merit tiers stayed about flat; tier criteria were unchanged, competitors made no changes to their published merit awards (C8), cost rose as the top reason in the decliner survey (C3), and the discount rate fell 47→41% (C15, E5).
E2 shows completed applications rose (9,850→10,240), admits rose (5,120→5,270) and mean admitted GPA rose (3.61→3.63); C7 shows only a negligible fall in regional graduates for 2026.

In C4, 51 of 64 document-status tickets were closed as 'document present after status refresh', and the vendor (C5) and Director (E4) describe a status-display lag; but 13 tickets were auto-closed with no resolution note, and the counsellor's claim (E3) cannot be checked because file-completion times are not in the export (C4).

C2 shows the yield drop was confined to the tiers whose awards were cut; Presidential (36.6→36.2%) and no-merit (38.5→37.0%) yields hardly moved, so demand did not soften for all groups alike, and C9 shows event attendance and satisfaction were stable.

C1's comparison between rounds shows the same yield drop in early action, where turnaround did not change, as in regular decision, where it slowed, so the turnaround difference is not linked to any difference in yield.

C2 gives a comparison with built-in controls (changed tiers vs unchanged Presidential and no-merit tiers, same eligibility criteria), with temporal order and mechanism (award cut printed on the admission letter, C14; finance decision, E5), competitor prices ruled out (C8), and turnaround ruled out by the EA/RD comparison (C1).

The reader freeze and the slowdown happened at the same time (C6, E2), but the scoring module was unavailable and unstable over the same period (C6, C13, C5); the records cannot separate the two, and nobody has measured which mattered (E4, C6).
The applicant pool was larger and academically stronger (E2), so it cannot explain lower enrolment; the shortfall came entirely through yield.
The shortfall is explained by the finance committee's merit schedule (C2, E5), not by Admissions turnaround (C1), so replacing the director would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place.

The yield loss is concentrated in the Dean's and Merit tiers whose awards were cut (C2), and total first-year net tuition fell 10.4% despite higher revenue per student (C15), so revisiting the schedule with the trade-off modelled before letters go out addresses the demonstrated cause.
The RD slowdown was real and drew service complaints (E2, E3, C3, C13), so a turnaround target is reasonable, but C1 shows it did not drive the yield drop, so it is not among the best actions.

Most 'missing document' tickets were resolved as a status-display lag (C4, C5), and an actual recording failure (H4) is unconfirmed, so ordering a rebuild under the remediation clause is not yet justified.

C2 and C1 together, supported by C8, C15 and E5, give a well-controlled pattern that pins the yield fall on the award cuts, which is enough to commit to taking the schedule back to the finance committee (A2).

ambiguousItems: S04: 'contradicted' is also defensible, since 51 of 64 tickets were display lag and the Director says every file was complete before review; but 13 tickets have no resolution, so 'unknown' fits the evidence.

S07: 'association-only' is also defensible for a reviewer who wants a direct intervention result; the tier comparison with unchanged control tiers plus C8 and C1 arguably meets the natural-experiment standard for 'causal'.

S06: some might answer 'unknown' because the RD delay applied only to merit-eligible files, which were also the tiers whose awards were cut; but the matched EA merit files had no delay and EA yield fell by the same amount, which supports 'contradicted'.
S12: 'acceptable' vs 'preferred' – fixing service quality is sensible regardless of the yield effect.
caseProblems: The presenting request limits collection to two items, and the decisive items (C1 by round, C2 by tier) are clearly labelled in their titles, so a solver can pick them from titles alone. This is mild leakage, though the titles do not state the results.

The case is internally consistent: the numbers reconcile (tier enrolments sum to 2,140 and 1,810; merit-eligible shares in C1 match the Dean's and Merit admit counts in C2; the +5.9% net revenue per student in C15 matches E5's projected +6%). No unrealistic data found.

In C5, the vendor attributes the late scoring module to Marrowbridge changing award amounts in December, which conflicts with E5's instruction to inform Admissions before EA decisions (15 Dec). This is a plausible but slightly odd detail; it does not affect the scoring.

rulings.explanation: Under the truth convention (initial evidence plus the read path C1, C2), the only evidence on H4 is E3 and E4. E3 is the counsellor's first-hand report of 'missing' transcripts despite upload confirmations. E4 is the Director's second-hand claim ('I'm told by the team') that every file was complete. She is an interested source, and her account is unverified. C1 and C2 say nothing about documents. So the evidence does not discriminate, and 'unknown' is correct. 'Contradicted' depends on C4, which is off-path. Even C4 does not count against H4: 51 tickets resolved as display lag leaves 13 auto-closed with no resolution, and the log has no file contents. Lag explaining most tickets does not rule out real loss in the rest. 'Supported' fails because E3 is one unverified anecdote that the Director disputes.

The edge-semantics definition of 'causal' explicitly lists 'temporal order plus mechanism plus covariation with the main rival ruled out'. All four parts are present on the read path. (1) Temporal order: the schedule was approved in Oct 2025 and applied to Fall 2026 offers (E5). (2) Mechanism: awards cut by $4,000–$5,000. (3) Covariation: about 13-point yield drops only in the cut tiers. Eligibility criteria were unchanged, and the Presidential and no-award control tiers held within 1.5 points (C2). (4) Main rival ruled out: EA admits had no delay, the merit-eligible share was the same in both rounds, and the EA and RD drops were the same (7.4 vs 7.5 points) (C1). The arithmetic also holds: non-merit tiers lost only about 10 enrolments in total, so EA's 140-student loss had to come mainly from the cut tiers, which were never slowed. General-market and applicant-pool rivals are excluded by C2 and E2. Asking for a direct intervention result sets a higher bar than the stated semantics, so 'association-only' does not fit the rubric.

C1 is a within-year comparison across rounds. EA merit-eligible files were decided on the old timetable (median 16 days), while RD merit-eligible files took a median 38 days. The merit-eligible mix was almost the same (54% vs 52%), and yield fell by the same amount in both rounds (7.4 vs 7.5 points). If slower turnaround had cut yield, RD would have fallen more. It did not, so the evidence counts against the link. The confound behind a possible 'unknown' (in RD, the slowed files and the cut tiers are the same students) is exactly what C1 removes, because EA merit files took the award cut without the delay. E3, and C3 off-path, are self-reports and cannot outweigh the behavioural comparison. 'Association-only' fails because the expected covariation across rounds is absent.

A3 targets a slowdown that is real (E2, E4) and that hurt counsellor relationships (E3), so it is reasonable and low-cost. That rules out 'harmful' and 'premature', since the slowdown itself is confirmed. But the president's question is about the enrolment shortfall, and C1 shows turnaround made no measurable difference to yield. A3 therefore does not address the established cause. A2 does, and it is the clearly best action. Two further points weaken A3 against 'preferred'. First, it sets a target without dealing with the unresolved bottleneck (frozen posts vs the scoring module, E4). Second, it routes monthly reporting to the provost, who is pursuing the wrong-party narrative. 'Sensible regardless' fits 'acceptable' (reasonable but not among the best), not 'preferred'.
